claim: Anatomical models of memory over the last 50 years have repeatedly highlighted the hippocampal inputs to the mammillary bodies via the postcommissural fornix.
source: Over the last 50 years, anatomical models of memory have repeatedly highlighted the hippocampal inputs to the mammillary bodies via the postcommissural fornix.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical focus of anatomical models, drawing on established scientific literature and consensus in the field.

claim: Anatomical models of memory downplay other projections to the mammillary bodies, leaving them largely ignored.
source: Such models downplay other projections to the mammillary bodies, leaving them largely ignored.
evidence: This is an inference based on the historical emphasis described in the manuscript and the literature.

claim: Only mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions impaired behavioral tests of spatial working memory.
source: Only mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions impaired behavioral tests of spatial working memory and, in particular, disrupted the use of extramaze spatial landmarks.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral test results presented in the manuscript, including T-maze alternation and radial-arm maze tasks.

claim: Mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions disrupted the use of extramaze spatial landmarks.
source: Only mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions impaired behavioral tests of spatial working memory and, in particular, disrupted the use of extramaze spatial landmarks.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data showing impairments when intra-maze cues were removed.

claim: Mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions produced widespread reductions in immediate-early gene (c-fos) expression in a network of memory-related regions.
source: The same lesions also produced widespread reductions in immediate-early gene (c-fos) expression in a network of memory-related regions, not seen after postcommissural fornix lesions.
evidence: This is supported by the c-Fos immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Postcommissural fornix lesions did not produce widespread reductions in c-fos expression in memory-related regions.
source: The same lesions also produced widespread reductions in immediate-early gene (c-fos) expression in a network of memory-related regions, not seen after postcommissural fornix lesions.
evidence: This is supported by the c-Fos data showing no significant reductions in the PCFx group compared to controls.

claim: The findings are inconsistent with previous models of mammillary body function dominated by hippocampal inputs.
source: These findings are inconsistent with previous models of mammillary body function (those dominated by hippocampal inputs) and herald a new understanding of why specific diencephalic structures are vital for memory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that PCFx lesions did not impair memory while VTNx and MTTx lesions did.

claim: The mammillary bodies are principally seen as a relay of hippocampal projections to the anterior thalamic nuclei.
source: Consequently, the mammillary bodies are principally seen as a relay of hippocampal projections to the anterior thalamic nuclei and, from there, to the cingulate (Barbizet, 1963; Delay and Brion, 1969) and prefrontal (Warrington and Weiskrantz, 1982) cortices.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature establishing this view.

claim: The mammillary bodies form part of an 'extended hippocampal system'.
source: The notion that the mammillary bodies form part of such an 'extended hippocampal system' (Aggleton and Brown, 1999) is seemingly supported by the unidirectional nature of the hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies (Aggleton et al., 2005), along with clinical evidence of the importance for memory of the mammillary body projections to the thalamus, via the mammillothalamic tract (MTT; Carlesimo et al., 2007; Van der Werf et al., 2000; Vann and Aggleton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical and clinical studies.

claim: Hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies are unidirectional.
source: The notion that the mammillary bodies form part of such an 'extended hippocampal system' (Aggleton and Brown, 1999) is seemingly supported by the unidirectional nature of the hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies (Aggleton et al., 2005), along with clinical evidence of the importance for memory of the mammillary body projections to the thalamus, via the mammillothalamic tract (MTT; Carlesimo et al., 2007; Van der Werf et al., 2000; Vann and Aggleton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to anatomical studies.

claim: Clinical evidence supports the importance for memory of the mammillary body projections to the thalamus via the mammillothalamic tract.
source: The notion that the mammillary bodies form part of such an 'extended hippocampal system' (Aggleton and Brown, 1999) is seemingly supported by the unidirectional nature of the hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies (Aggleton et al., 2005), along with clinical evidence of the importance for memory of the mammillary body projections to the thalamus, via the mammillothalamic tract (MTT; Carlesimo et al., 2007; Van der Werf et al., 2000; Vann and Aggleton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Standard models of mammillary body function provide no real function for the mammillary bodies.
source: However, these standard models suffer two major shortcomings. First, they provide no real function for the mammillary bodies and second, they ignore other mammillary body afferents.
evidence: This is a critical inference based on the author's analysis of existing models.

claim: Standard models of mammillary body function ignore other mammillary body afferents.
source: However, these standard models suffer two major shortcomings. First, they provide no real function for the mammillary bodies and second, they ignore other mammillary body afferents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review and the focus of previous models.

claim: The mammillary bodies receive dense inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei.
source: The mammillary bodies receive dense inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei (e.g., Takeuchi et al., 1985), making it possible that these midbrain inputs are functionally important for memory (Vann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to anatomical studies.

claim: Midbrain inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei may be functionally important for memory.
source: The mammillary bodies receive dense inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei (e.g., Takeuchi et al., 1985), making it possible that these midbrain inputs are functionally important for memory (Vann, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation and the rationale for the current study.

claim: Postcommissural fornix lesions disconnect the hippocampal formation projections to the mammillary bodies whilst leaving other hippocampal connections intact.
source: In one group the descending postcommissural fornix (PCF) was lesioned, a procedure that disconnects the hippocampal formation projections to the mammillary bodies whilst leaving other hippocampal connections intact, including those with the septum, striatum and anterior thalamic nuclei (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study demonstrating this anatomical specificity.

claim: Postcommissural fornix lesions leave hippocampal connections with the septum, striatum and anterior thalamic nuclei intact.
source: In one group the descending postcommissural fornix (PCF) was lesioned, a procedure that disconnects the hippocampal formation projections to the mammillary bodies whilst leaving other hippocampal connections intact, including those with the septum, striatum and anterior thalamic nuclei (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to anatomical studies.

claim: The lateral mammillary nucleus receives dense inputs from Gudden's dorsal tegmental nucleus.
source: Although the lateral mammillary nucleus receives dense inputs from Gudden's dorsal tegmental nucleus, the VTNg was targeted because of its inputs to the medial mammillary nucleus.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden provides inputs to the medial mammillary nucleus.
source: Although the lateral mammillary nucleus receives dense inputs from Gudden's dorsal tegmental nucleus, the VTNg was targeted because of its inputs to the medial mammillary nucleus.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Previous clinical and behavioral evidence highlights the particular importance of the medial mammillary nucleus for memory.
source: Previous clinical and behavioral evidence highlights the particular importance of the medial mammillary nucleus for memory (Vann, 2005, 2010, 2011; Vann and Albasser, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T-maze alternation and radial-arm maze working memory tasks are sensitive to hippocampal damage.
source: Rats were tested on three behavioral tasks, the first two of which are sensitive to hippocampal damage: T-maze alternation, a working memory task in the radial-arm maze, and a geometric discrimination task (Aggleton et al., 2009; Vann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MTT lesions result in widespread neural hypoactivity, as measured by expression of the immediate-early gene c-fos.
source: In addition to impairing spatial memory, MTT lesions also result in widespread neural hypoactivity, as measured by expression of the immediate-early gene c-fos (Vann and Albasser, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The final study groups comprised seven Gudden's ventral tegmental nuclei lesion animals (VTNx), eight mammillothalamic tract lesion animals (MTTx), seven postcommissural fornix lesions (PCFx) and eight surgical controls (Sham).
source: A stringent lesion criterion was adopted for final inclusion in the study and, as a consequence, the final groups comprised seven Gudden's ventral tegmental nuclei lesion animals (VTNx), eight mammillothalamic tract lesion animals (MTTx), seven postcommissural fornix lesions (PCFx) and eight surgical controls (Sham).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental groups and sample sizes.

claim: VTNg lesions produced a clear loss of the large, distinctive cells in the ventral tegmental nucleus.
source: The VTNg lesions, which were assessed using Nissl and acetylcholinesterase stained sections (Figure 1A,B), produced a clear loss of the large, distinctive cells in the ventral tegmental nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by histological assessment and reference to Figure 1A,B.

claim: In all VTNx animals there was very limited damage to the medial-most part of the oral part of the reticular pontine nucleus.
source: In all animals there was very limited damage to the medial-most part of the oral part of the reticular pontine nucleus; this damage was always unilateral and on the contralateral side of the brain to that in which the needle was inserted to make the lesion.
evidence: This is based on histological assessment of the lesions.

claim: Damage to the reticular pontine nucleus in VTNx animals was always unilateral and on the contralateral side of the brain to that in which the needle was inserted.
source: In all animals there was very limited damage to the medial-most part of the oral part of the reticular pontine nucleus; this damage was always unilateral and on the contralateral side of the brain to that in which the needle was inserted to make the lesion.
evidence: This is based on histological assessment.

claim: There was a restricted loss of cells in the most dorsal part of the median raphe nuclei at the level of the VTNg.
source: At just this level there was a restricted loss of cells in the most dorsal part of the median raphe nuclei, that is, limited to just that part directly adjacent to the VTNg.
evidence: This is based on histological assessment.

claim: There was no evidence that the VTNx lesions extended into either Gudden's dorsal tegmental nuclei or the laterodorsal tegmental nuclei.
source: There was no evidence that the lesions extended into either Gudden's dorsal tegmental nuclei or the laterodorsal tegmental nuclei, both of which stained intensely for acetylcholinesterase.
evidence: This is based on histological assessment using acetylcholinesterase staining.

claim: The laterodorsal tegmental nucleus is the sole source of anterior thalamic cholinergic innervations.
source: The integrity of the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus is important, being the sole source of anterior thalamic cholinergic innervations and a major source of interpeduncular cholinergic inputs (Satoh and Fibiger, 1986; Sikes and Vogt, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The laterodorsal tegmental nucleus is a major source of interpeduncular cholinergic inputs.
source: The integrity of the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus is important, being the sole source of anterior thalamic cholinergic innervations and a major source of interpeduncular cholinergic inputs (Satoh and Fibiger, 1986; Sikes and Vogt, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The laterodorsal tegmental nuclei and their cholinergic projections were intact in VTNx animals.
source: The observation that the laterodorsal tegmental nuclei, and subsequently their cholinergic projections, were intact was confirmed by assessing the level of acetylcholinesterase staining in the anteroventral thalamic nucleus (Figure 1C,D) and interpeduncular nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by acetylcholinesterase staining data and reference to Figure 1C,D.

claim: Fornix section leads to shrinkage of the mammillary bodies due to loss of white matter.
source: It has been repeatedly shown that fornix section leads to shrinkage of the mammillary bodies (due to loss of white matter).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The mean mammillary body area for the PCFx group was 1.34 mm2 ± 0.031, significantly smaller than the Sham group measurements of 1.79 mm2 ± 0.058.
source: The mean mammillary body area (±SEM) for the PCFx group was 1.34 mm2 ± 0.031, making them significantly smaller than the Sham group measurements of 1.79 mm2 ± 0.058 (t(13) = 6.44; p<0.001; Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1G,H.

claim: The reduced mammillary body volumes of the PCFx lesion cohort did not differ from a previous cohort where retrograde tracers had been used to confirm the postcommissural fornix disconnection.
source: Furthermore, the reduced mammillary body volumes of the present PCFx lesion cohort did not differ from a previous cohort where retrograde tracers had been used to confirm the postcommissural fornix disconnection (t(14)=1.67; p>0.1) or from rats with complete fornix lesions (t < 1) (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison with previous data.

claim: The reduced mammillary body volumes of the PCFx lesion cohort did not differ from rats with complete fornix lesions.
source: Furthermore, the reduced mammillary body volumes of the present PCFx lesion cohort did not differ from a previous cohort where retrograde tracers had been used to confirm the postcommissural fornix disconnection (t(14)=1.67; p>0.1) or from rats with complete fornix lesions (t < 1) (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison with previous data.

claim: The mammillary body cross-sectional area differed significantly among all four groups.
source: When considering the mammillary body cross-sectional area of all four groups in the study there was a main effect of group (F(3,27) = 22.3, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The mammillary bodies were larger in the Sham group than all lesion groups.
source: Post-hoc comparisons revealed the mammillary bodies to be larger in the Sham group than all lesion groups (all p<0.001) while none of the lesion groups differed significantly from each other (all p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical comparisons.

claim: None of the lesion groups differed significantly from each other in mammillary body cross-sectional area.
source: Post-hoc comparisons revealed the mammillary bodies to be larger in the Sham group than all lesion groups (all p<0.001) while none of the lesion groups differed significantly from each other (all p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical comparisons.

claim: There was a significant increase in cell packing in the PCFx lesion group compared to all three other groups.
source: There was an overall group effect (F(3,27) = 9.96, p<0.001) which reflected a significant increase in the cell packing in the PCFx lesion group compared to all three other groups (Sham, p<0.01; MTTx, p<0.005; VTNx, p<0.001) there was no difference in cell packing in any of the other groups (all comparisons, p>0.5).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data and statistical analysis.

claim: The reduced mammillary body volume in the PCFx group reflects loss of white matter and not an overall change in neuronal numbers.
source: This is consistent with the reduced mammillary body volume in the PCFx group reflecting loss of white matter and not an overall change in neuronal numbers (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell packing data and reference to Figure 1I,J.

claim: Lack of difference in cell packing in the MTTx and VTNx groups, combined with reduced cross-sectional area, is consistent with some medial mammillary body cell loss in these groups.
source: In contrast, lack of difference in cell packing in the MTTx and VTNx groups, combined with reduced cross-sectional area, would be consistent with some medial mammillary body cell loss in these groups.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell packing and area measurements.

claim: Rats can use multiple cue-types to perform spatial alternation tasks.
source: Rats can use multiple cue-types to perform spatial alternation tasks (e.g., Douglas, 1966; Dudchenko, 2001), including visual allocentric cues, intra-maze cues (e.g., odor trails), directional cues (i.e., bearing), and egocentric cues (i.e., body turns).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There was an overall effect of lesion in Stage 1 of T-maze alternation.
source: There was an overall effect of lesion (F(3,27) = 4.93, p=0.007; Figure 2B) and an overall effect of training block (F(1.44,38.9) = 3.50, p=0.037) but no lesion group x block interaction (F(4.33,38.9) = 1.52, p>0.1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The performance of the VTNx group was significantly worse than the Sham group in Stage 1 of T-maze alternation.
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed the performance of the VTNx group to be significantly worse than the Sham group (p=0.005).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant overall group effect on Stage 2 of T-maze alternation.
source: There was a significant, overall group effect on Stage 2 (F(3,27) = 7.12, p=0.001; Figure 2B) but no effect of block (F < 1) and no group x block interaction (F < 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The MTTx and VTNx groups had significantly lower scores than the Sham group in Stage 2 of T-maze alternation.
source: The group effect reflected the lower scores of both the MTTx (p=0.004) and VTNx (p=0.006) groups compared to the Sham rats.
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: The lack of impairment in the MTTx group in Stage 1 reflected their use of intra-maze cues.
source: These results suggest that the lack of impairment in the MTTx group in Stage 1 reflected their use of intra-maze cues, such as odor trails.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of impairments across stages.

claim: Same place trials were more difficult than different place trials in Stage 2 of T-maze alternation.
source: Overall, same place trials were more difficult than different place trials (F(1,27) = 25.4, p<0.001) but no there was trial type x group interaction (F(3,27) = 1.23, p>0.3; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: There were group differences in Stage 3 of T-maze alternation.
source: An overall analysis of Stage 3 revealed group differences (F(3,27) = 6.28, p=0.002) but no effect of block (F(3,81) = 2.19, p>0.3) and no block x group interaction (F(9,81) = 1.08, p>0.3; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1B (likely Figure 2B based on context).

claim: The performances of the VTNx and MTTx groups were significantly worse than those of both the Sham group and the PCFx group in Stage 3 of T-maze alternation.
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the performances of the VTNx and MTTx groups were significantly worse than those of both the Sham group (VTNx, p=0.025; MTTx, p=0.019) and the PCFx group (VTNx, p=0.029; MTTx, p=0.023).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: The lack of a trial type effect in Stage 3 is expected if being in the dark removed the visual cues that had previously helped the rats to discriminate food well locations.
source: The lack of a trial type effect ('same' vs 'different' F(1,27) = 3.60, p>0.05) is to be expected if being in the dark removed the visual cues that had previously helped the rats to discriminate food well locations (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental manipulation and results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: There was a significant effect of group on total errors in the radial-arm maze acquisition phase.
source: For the acquisition phase (Stage 1) there was a significant effect of group using both errors (F(3,27) = 6.20, p=0.002; Figure 3A) and correct entries (F(3,27) = 6.54, p=0.002; Figure 3B); in both instances post-hoc comparisons showed this group effect to be due to significant differences between the Sham group and both the MTTx (errors, p=0.007; entries, p=0.005) and VTNx groups (errors, p=0.005; entries, p=0.004).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The MTTx and VTNx groups made significantly more errors than the Sham group in the radial-arm maze acquisition phase.
source: For the acquisition phase (Stage 1) there was a significant effect of group using both errors (F(3,27) = 6.20, p=0.002; Figure 3A) and correct entries (F(3,27) = 6.54, p=0.002; Figure 3B); in both instances post-hoc comparisons showed this group effect to be due to significant differences between the Sham group and both the MTTx (errors, p=0.007; entries, p=0.005) and VTNx groups (errors, p=0.005; entries, p=0.004).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The MTTx and VTNx groups had significantly fewer correct entries than the Sham group in the radial-arm maze acquisition phase.
source: For the acquisition phase (Stage 1) there was a significant effect of group using both errors (F(3,27) = 6.20, p=0.002; Figure 3A) and correct entries (F(3,27) = 6.54, p=0.002; Figure 3B); in both instances post-hoc comparisons showed this group effect to be due to significant differences between the Sham group and both the MTTx (errors, p=0.007; entries, p=0.005) and VTNx groups (errors, p=0.005; entries, p=0.004).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Following maze rotation, the groups significantly differed in terms of number of errors made.
source: Following this manipulation the groups significantly differed in terms of number of errors made (F(3,27) = 6.35, p=0.002; Figure 3A) and correct entries in the first eight choices (F(3,27) = 6.80, p=0.001; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Following maze rotation, the MTTx and VTNx groups made significantly more errors than the Sham group.
source: Post-hoc comparisons revealed this group effect to be due to differences between the Sham group and both the MTTx (errors, p=0.007; entries, p=0.015) and VTNx groups (errors, p=0.023; entries, p=0.022).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: Following maze rotation, there were significant differences between the PCFx and MTTx scores using both error and correct entry values.
source: In addition, there were significant differences between the PCFx and MTTx scores using both error and correct entry values (errors, p=0.030; entries, p=0.014) and between the PCFx and VTNx groups using correct entries (p=0.020).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: There was no difference between any of the groups' escape latencies for the pre-training session in the circular pool.
source: There was no difference between any of the groups' escape latencies for this pre-training session in the circular pool (F(3,27) = 1.48, p>0.2; means ± SEM, MTTx = 26.1 ± 3.1 VTNx = 31.8 ± 3.6; PCFx = 23.6 ± 2.2; Sham = 29.7 ± 2.5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: All groups of rats were able to learn the geometric discrimination task.
source: All groups of rats were able to learn this task as demonstrated by a lack of group effect (F(3,27) = 2.38, p>0.05), a significant effect of training block (F(3,81) = 62.8, p<0.001; Figure 4B) and no group x block interaction (F < 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: There were no group differences in swim velocity during acquisition of the geometric discrimination task.
source: There were no group differences in swim velocity during acquisition (F(3,27) = 2.44, p>0.05) nor was there a group x training block interaction (F(10.1,91.3) = 1.59, p>0.1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: All groups had clearly learnt to discriminate the geometry of the rectangle as reflected by significantly longer time spent in the correct corners compared to incorrect corners.
source: There was no effect of group (F < 1) but all groups had clearly learnt to discriminate the geometry of the rectangle as reflected by a significantly longer time spent in the correct corners compared to incorrect corners (F(1,27) = 207.8, p<0.001; Figure 4C) and lack of group by corner interaction (F(3,27) = 2.43, p>0.05; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4C.

claim: There was a significant group effect in c-Fos counts in the retrosplenial cortex.
source: There was a significant group effect (F(3,26) = 11.97, p<0.001; Figure 5A) as the Sham group had more Fos-positive cells compared to both the MTTx (p<0.001) and VTNx groups (p=0.006).
evidence: This is supported by c-Fos count data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The Sham group had more Fos-positive cells in the retrosplenial cortex compared to both the MTTx and VTNx groups.
source: There was a significant group effect (F(3,26) = 11.97, p<0.001; Figure 5A) as the Sham group had more Fos-positive cells compared to both the MTTx (p<0.001) and VTNx groups (p=0.006).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: There were significantly more Fos-positive cells in the retrosplenial cortex in the PCFx lesion group relative to both the MTTx and VTNx lesion groups.
source: There were also significantly more Fos-positive cells in the PCFx lesion group relative to both the MTTx (p=0.001) and VTNx lesion (p=0.026) groups (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis and reference to Figure 6.

claim: There was a main group effect in hippocampal Fos-positive cell counts.
source: There was a main group effect (F(3,26) = 5.52, p=0.05; Figure 5A) as c-Fos counts in the Sham group were significantly higher than both the MTTx group (p=0.029) and VTNx groups (p=0.009).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: c-Fos counts in the hippocampus in the Sham group were significantly higher than both the MTTx group and VTNx groups.
source: There was a main group effect (F(3,26) = 5.52, p=0.05; Figure 5A) as c-Fos counts in the Sham group were significantly higher than both the MTTx group (p=0.029) and VTNx groups (p=0.009).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The lesion-induced changes in hippocampal c-fos expression appeared to be largely driven by reductions in CA1.
source: These analyses revealed that the lesion-induced changes in hippocampual c-fos expression appeared to be largely driven by reductions in CA1 as this was the only subfield where there was a significant group difference (dentate gyrus: F < 1; CA3: F(3,26) =2.01, p>0.4; CA1: F(3,26) =8.07, p<0.005).
evidence: This is an inference based on subfield-specific statistical analyses.

claim: The group difference in CA1 arose due to fewer Fos-positive cell counts in both the MTTx and VTNx groups compared to the Sham group.
source: The group difference in CA1 arose due to fewer Fos-positive cell counts in both the MTTx and VTNx groups compared to the Sham group (both p<0.005).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: There was no group effect when analysing the infralimbic cortex.
source: There was no group effect when analysing the infralimbic cortex (F(3,26) =1.23, p>0.3; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Analyses of the prelimbic cortex revealed an overall group effect.
source: In contrast, analyses of the prelimbic cortex revealed an overall group effect (F(3,26) = 5.32, p=0.006; Figure 5B) as significantly fewer c-Fos positive cells were found in the MTTx ( p=0.041) and VTNx (p=0.017) groups than in the Sham group.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Significantly fewer c-Fos positive cells were found in the prelimbic cortex in the MTTx and VTNx groups than in the Sham group.
source: In contrast, analyses of the prelimbic cortex revealed an overall group effect (F(3,26) = 5.32, p=0.006; Figure 5B) as significantly fewer c-Fos positive cells were found in the MTTx ( p=0.041) and VTNx (p=0.017) groups than in the Sham group.
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: There was no group effect for somatosensory cortex, supramammillary nucleus, lateral or medial septum in c-Fos counts.
source: There was no group effect for somatosensory cortex (F < 1; Figure 5C), supramammillary nucleus, lateral or medial septum (all F < 1; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Models of MB function have inevitably focused on their dense hippocampal inputs.
source: Although the mammillary bodies (MBs) have a very longstanding association with memory (Gudden, 1896), remarkably little is known about their specific contributions. Models of MB function have inevitably focused on their dense hippocampal inputs (Aggleton and Brown, 1999) so that the MBs are principally thought to relay hippocampal information to the anterior thalamic nuclei (via the mammillothalamic tract), and then beyond (e.g., Barbizet, 1963; Delay and Brion, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous models and literature.

claim: The MBs are principally thought to relay hippocampal information to the anterior thalamic nuclei via the mammillothalamic tract.
source: Models of MB function have inevitably focused on their dense hippocampal inputs (Aggleton and Brown, 1999) so that the MBs are principally thought to relay hippocampal information to the anterior thalamic nuclei (via the mammillothalamic tract), and then beyond (e.g., Barbizet, 1963; Delay and Brion, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous models.

claim: The MBs have heavy, reciprocal connections with Gudden's tegmental nuclei whose functional significance has been largely overlooked.
source: However, the MBs have heavy, reciprocal connections with Gudden's tegmental nuclei whose functional significance has been largely overlooked.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge and the author's assessment of the literature.

claim: Mammillothalamic tract lesions cause c-Fos hypoactivity in numerous sites including the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex.
source: The second goal arose because mammillothalamic tract lesions cause c-Fos hypoactivity in numerous sites including the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex (Vann and Albasser, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden is reciprocally connected with the medial mammillary nucleus.
source: The present study focused on the ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden as it is reciprocally connected with the medial mammillary nucleus while the dorsal tegmental nucleus connects with the lateral mammillary nucleus.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The dorsal tegmental nucleus connects with the lateral mammillary nucleus.
source: The present study focused on the ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden as it is reciprocally connected with the medial mammillary nucleus while the dorsal tegmental nucleus connects with the lateral mammillary nucleus.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The lateral mammillary nucleus forms part of the head-direction network.
source: Although the lateral mammillary nucleus forms part of the head-direction network (e.g., Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Hopkins, 2005), it is the loss of the medial mammillary system that appears principally responsible for the spatial memory impairments associated with complete lesions of this structure (Vann, 2005, 2010, 2011; Vann and Albasser, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is the loss of the medial mammillary system that appears principally responsible for the spatial memory impairments associated with complete lesions of the mammillary bodies.
source: Although the lateral mammillary nucleus forms part of the head-direction network (e.g., Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Hopkins, 2005), it is the loss of the medial mammillary system that appears principally responsible for the spatial memory impairments associated with complete lesions of this structure (Vann, 2005, 2010, 2011; Vann and Albasser, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The medial mammillary nucleus is always atrophied in the amnesic Korsakoff's syndrome.
source: Furthermore, it is the medial mammillary nucleus that is always atrophied in the amnesic Korsakoff's syndrome (Victor et al., 1989; Kopelman, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Only the MTTx and VTNx groups were impaired on the behavioral tasks relative to the Sham groups.
source: In contrast to the predictions of traditional models of MB function (e.g., Delay and Brion, 1969; Gaffan, 1992; Aggleton and Brown, 1999), only the MTTx and VTNx groups were impaired on the behavioral tasks relative to the Sham groups.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results across all tasks.

claim: The MTTx and VTNx groups did not significantly differ from one another in behavioral performance.
source: At no stage did these two lesion groups significantly differ from one another.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparisons across all behavioral tasks.

claim: The MTTx group had been using intra-maze cues to solve Stage 1 of T-maze alternation, masking their spatial memory impairments.
source: The performances of the VTNx and MTTx groups in Stage 2 were equivalent, with both groups impaired relative to the Sham group, suggesting the MTTx group had been using intra-maze cues to solve Stage 1, so masking their spatial memory impairments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results across stages.

claim: Both behavioral tasks indicated that the MTTx and VTNx rats were less able to use allocentric cues and more reliant on intra-maze cues.
source: Thus both behavioral tasks indicated that the MTTx and VTNx rats were less able to use allocentric cues and more reliant on intra-maze cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral results from both T-maze and radial-arm maze tasks.

claim: The PCFx animals were not impaired relative to the Shams on any of the behavioral tasks.
source: In contrast, the PCFx animals were not impaired relative to the Shams on any of the behavioral tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results for the PCFx group.

claim: The PCFx animals performed significantly better than both the VTNx and MTTx groups on both the radial-arm maze and T-maze tasks.
source: Consequently, the PCFx animals performed significantly better than both the VTNx and MTTx groups on both the radial-arm maze and T-maze tasks despite producing MB shrinkage (resulting from loss of fiber inputs) equivalent to that found after complete fornix lesions.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons of behavioral performance.

claim: The present PCFx lesions were indistinguishable from those that had previously been demonstrated to completely disconnect the hippocampal formation-MB projections.
source: The present PCFx lesions were indistinguishable from those that had previously been demonstrated to completely disconnect the hippocampal formation-MB projections (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous anatomical validation studies.

claim: The pattern of behavioral impairments was paralleled by the c-Fos findings.
source: The pattern of behavioral impairments was paralleled by the c-Fos findings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correspondence between behavioral and c-Fos results.

claim: Both the VTNx and MTTx groups had significantly fewer c-Fos positive cells in the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex.
source: Both the VTNx and MTTx groups had significantly fewer c-Fos positive cells in the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and prelimbic cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the c-Fos results.

claim: Reduced levels of c-Fos have been found in the same network of brain regions following anterior thalamic nuclei lesions.
source: Reduced levels of c-Fos have also been found in this same network of brain regions following anterior thalamic nuclei lesions (Jenkins et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The MTT and VTNg lesions do not result in direct de-afferentation of the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, or prelimbic cortex.
source: However, unlike the c-Fos reduction following anterior thalamic lesions, the current changes reflect 'indirect' effects, as the MTT and VTNg lesions do not result in direct de-afferentation of any of these sites.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge of the connections.

claim: Reduced activity in memory-related networks seems to be a consistent marker of damage to the medial diencephalon in animal models and humans.
source: Although reduced activity in this memory-related network seems to be a consistent marker of damage to the medial diencephalon, in animal models and humans (Joyce et al., 1994; Kapur, 1994; Reed et al., 2003; Savage et al., 2003; Caulo et al., 2005; Anzalone et al., 2010), it is not known whether this reduced activity contributes to mnemonic deficits or whether it simply a symptom of the system no longer working effectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is not known whether reduced activity in memory-related networks contributes to mnemonic deficits or is simply a symptom of the system no longer working effectively.
source: Although reduced activity in this memory-related network seems to be a consistent marker of damage to the medial diencephalon, in animal models and humans (Joyce et al., 1994; Kapur, 1994; Reed et al., 2003; Savage et al., 2003; Caulo et al., 2005; Anzalone et al., 2010), it is not known whether this reduced activity contributes to mnemonic deficits or whether it simply a symptom of the system no longer working effectively.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Evidence for reduced c-Fos activity contributing to mnemonic deficits comes from learning and memory deficits found after infusions of antisense that block c-Fos activity.
source: Evidence for the former account comes learning and memory deficits found after infusions of antisense that block c-Fos activity (He et al., 2002; Seoane et al., 2012; Katche et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The present PCFx lesion findings were remarkably similar to those found previously.
source: The present PCFx lesion findings were remarkably similar to those found previously (Vann et al., 2011), for example, they resulted in a 5% reduction in accuracy of T-maze alternation.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous data.

claim: PCFx lesions resulted in a 5% reduction in accuracy of T-maze alternation.
source: The present PCFx lesion findings were remarkably similar to those found previously (Vann et al., 2011), for example, they resulted in a 5% reduction in accuracy of T-maze alternation.
evidence: This is based on the behavioral data.

claim: It is possible that the tasks used in the present study did not sufficiently tax the postcommissural fornix pathway.
source: It is possible that the tasks used in the present study did not sufficiently tax this pathway and that greater task demands could result in lesion-induced impairments.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations.

claim: The general lack of effects following PCFx lesions may be due to redundancies in this pathway, given the direct projections from the hippocampal formation to the anterior thalamic nuclei.
source: In addition, it may be that these projections contribute to memory under normal conditions but the general lack of effects following PCFx lesions are due to redundancies in this pathway, given the direct projections from the hippocampal formation to the anterior thalamic nuclei.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of PCFx lesion effects.

claim: The hippocampal projections to the MBs and anterior thalamic nuclei arise from different cell populations.
source: The hippocampal projections to the MBs and anterior thalamic nuclei arise from different cell populations (Wright et al., 2010) so it is not clear whether the same information is being conveyed (Tsanov et al., 2011) and, therefore, how much replication there is in the system.
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: It is not clear whether the same information is being conveyed by hippocampal projections to the MBs and anterior thalamic nuclei.
source: The hippocampal projections to the MBs and anterior thalamic nuclei arise from different cell populations (Wright et al., 2010) so it is not clear whether the same information is being conveyed (Tsanov et al., 2011) and, therefore, how much replication there is in the system.
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Examples where fornix lesions appear more disruptive than MB lesions are consistent with the idea that the direct hippocampal-thalamic inputs are supportive.
source: Those examples where fornix lesions appear more disruptive than MB lesions (Aggleton et al., 1995; Gaffan et al., 2001) are consistent with the idea that the direct hippocampal-thalamic inputs are supportive, but there are some situations where anterior thalamic or MB lesion effects can be greater than those of fornix lesions (Tonkiss and Rawlins, 1992; Vann et al., 2000; Jenkins et al., 2004; Aggleton et al., 2009), so highlighting the potential functional importance of additional information streams, for example, from the limbic midbrain.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies.

claim: There are some situations where anterior thalamic or MB lesion effects can be greater than those of fornix lesions.
source: Those examples where fornix lesions appear more disruptive than MB lesions (Aggleton et al., 1995; Gaffan et al., 2001) are consistent with the idea that the direct hippocampal-thalamic inputs are supportive, but there are some situations where anterior thalamic or MB lesion effects can be greater than those of fornix lesions (Tonkiss and Rawlins, 1992; Vann et al., 2000; Jenkins et al., 2004; Aggleton et al., 2009), so highlighting the potential functional importance of additional information streams, for example, from the limbic midbrain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The present findings clearly suggest that the more crucial inputs for MB spatial function are from VTNg rather than the hippocampal formation.
source: The present findings clearly suggest that the more crucial inputs for MB spatial function are from VTNg rather than the hippocampal formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral and c-Fos results.

claim: VTNg cells fire rhythmically and coherently with hippocampal theta.
source: VTNg cells fire rhythmically and coherently with hippocampal theta (Kocsis et al., 2001), and theta-related cells in the medial mammillary nucleus have been linked to memory function (Alonso and Llinas, 1992; Kocsis and Vertes, 1994; Bland et al., 1995; Kirk et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: Theta-related cells in the medial mammillary nucleus have been linked to memory function.
source: VTNg cells fire rhythmically and coherently with hippocampal theta (Kocsis et al., 2001), and theta-related cells in the medial mammillary nucleus have been linked to memory function (Alonso and Llinas, 1992; Kocsis and Vertes, 1994; Bland et al., 1995; Kirk et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The VTNg have been linked to vigilance states.
source: It is also the case that the VTNg have been linked to vigilance states (Bassant and Poindessous-Jazat, 2001), and so might additionally modulate hippocampal activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The VTNg might modulate hippocampal activity.
source: It is also the case that the VTNg have been linked to vigilance states (Bassant and Poindessous-Jazat, 2001), and so might additionally modulate hippocampal activity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known functions of VTNg.

claim: The presumption, based on dense interconnectivity, is that the VTNg lesion effects are primarily via the MBs.
source: The presumption, based on their dense interconnectivity, is that the VTNg lesion effects are primarily via the MBs.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The VTNg innervates a number of other sites, including the lateral hypothalamus, preoptic area, medial septum, parts of the reticular pontine nucleus, median raphe nuclei, supramammillary nucleus and ventral tegmental area.
source: The VTNg does, however, innervate a number of other sites, including the lateral hypothalamus, preoptic area, medial septum, parts of the reticular pontine nucleus, median raphe nuclei, supramammillary nucleus and ventral tegmental area (Petrovicky, 1973; Leichnetz et al., 1989; Hayakawa et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Other VTNg efferents appear light.
source: These other VTNg efferents appear light (see Hayakawa and Zyo, 1984), and in some instances not been confirmed (Barone et al., 1981; Vertes, 1988), a contribution from their disconnection must be considered, particularly because some of these other sites have hippocampal connections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Lesions of alternative VTNg projection sites rarely result in the pattern of spatial memory impairments seen following VTNg lesions.
source: However, lesions of these alternative sites rarely result in the pattern of spatial memory impairments seen following VTNg lesions (e.g., Sarihi et al., 2000; Pan and McNaughton, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous lesion studies.

claim: The lack of Fos changes in the supramammillary and septal nuclei following VTNg lesions provides evidence that VTNg lesions are not having their effects via these routes.
source: In addition, the lack of Fos changes in the supramammillary and septal nuclei following VTNg lesions provides some evidence that they are not having their effects via these routes, while the striking similarity of the VTNg and MTT lesion effects in the present study provides further support for the VTNg-MB pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the c-Fos data.

claim: The striking similarity of the VTNg and MTT lesion effects provides support for the VTNg-MB pathway.
source: In addition, the lack of Fos changes in the supramammillary and septal nuclei following VTNg lesions provides some evidence that they are not having their effects via these routes, while the striking similarity of the VTNg and MTT lesion effects in the present study provides further support for the VTNg-MB pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of behavioral and c-Fos results.

claim: The MTT and VTNg lesion effects appear to be selective for spatial working memory and not due to non-specific effects such as loss of arousal or motivation.
source: In rats, the MTT and VTNg lesion effects appear to be selective for spatial working memory and not due to non-specific effects such as loss of arousal or motivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results across different tasks.

claim: Both MTTx and VTNx groups were able to acquire a geometric discrimination task at the same rate, and to the same level, as the Sham group.
source: Both MTTx and VTNx groups were able to acquire a geometric discrimination task at the same rate, and to the same level, as the Sham group.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data from the water-maze task.

claim: The geometric discrimination task may be particularly sensitive to lesions within the head-direction system.
source: This task may be particularly sensitive to lesions within the head-direction system (Aggleton et al., 2009; Vann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The MTT lesions in the present study are most likely to disconnect the medial MB efferents, while leaving many lateral MB efferents largely intact.
source: As the MTT lesions in the present study are most likely to disconnect the medial MB efferents, while leaving many lateral MB efferents largely intact (Vann and Albasser, 2009) this sparing provides further support for the dissociation of two memory systems within the MBs (Allen and Hopkins, 1989; Vann and Aggleton, 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge and cited studies.

claim: The sparing of geometric discrimination performance provides support for the dissociation of two memory systems within the MBs.
source: As the MTT lesions in the present study are most likely to disconnect the medial MB efferents, while leaving many lateral MB efferents largely intact (Vann and Albasser, 2009) this sparing provides further support for the dissociation of two memory systems within the MBs (Allen and Hopkins, 1989; Vann and Aggleton, 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results and cited studies.

claim: Clinical studies show that both the MBs and the MTT are important for human memory, and recollective memory in particular.
source: Clinical studies show that both the MBs and the MTT are important for human memory, and recollective memory in particular (Dusoir et al., 1990; Van der Werf et al., 2000; Carlesimo et al., 2007; Tsivilis et al., 2008; Vann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The situation regarding the human VTNg is far less clear.
source: The situation regarding the human VTNg is far less clear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: For a number of years the very existence of the VTNg in humans had been in doubt.
source: Indeed, for a number of years the very existence of this nucleus in humans had been in doubt (Petrovicky, 1971; Hayakawa and Zyo, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The structure and connections of the VTNg are remarkably similar across species.
source: However, it is now apparent that the structure and connections of the VTNg are remarkably similar across species (Petrovicky, 1973; Irle and Markowitsch, 1982; Hayakawa and Zyo, 1984; Huang et al., 1992; Saunders et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative anatomical studies.

claim: There is only one reported amnesic patient with restricted damage in the VTN area.
source: To date, there is only one reported amnesic patient with restricted damage in the VTN area, but this study is limited in that only CT images were available (Goldberg et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical case study.

claim: The current findings support a novel model of limbic brain interactions.
source: The current findings support a novel model of limbic brain interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall results of the study.

claim: The MBs have important roles in memory that can be independent of their hippocampal inputs.
source: They show that the MBs have important roles in memory that can be independent of their hippocampal inputs; instead, the results highlight the VTNg.
evidence: This is a key conclusion based on the data showing VTNx and MTTx impairments but not PCFx impairments.

claim: MTT and VTNg lesions result in strikingly similar spatial memory impairments.
source: Not only do MTT and VTNg lesions result in strikingly similar spatial memory impairments but they also both result in widespread hypoactivity across a memory-related network.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results.

claim: MTT and VTNg lesions both result in widespread hypoactivity across a memory-related network.
source: Not only do MTT and VTNg lesions result in strikingly similar spatial memory impairments but they also both result in widespread hypoactivity across a memory-related network.
evidence: This is a summary of the c-Fos results.

claim: These findings highlight the importance of looking beyond the hippocampus to larger networks of brain regions that contribute to memory.
source: These findings highlight the importance of looking beyond the hippocampus to larger networks of brain regions that contribute to memory (Vann and Albasser, 2011).
evidence: This is a broader implication of the findings, supported by a citation.
